To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the function of GluD2-NMDARs, which mediate LTP in wild-type mice, becomes altered during early pathology in PS2APP mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, and that this alteration is reflected in the unusual requirement for GluN2A-NMDARs during LTP and the impaired LTD in these models.

GluN2A and GluN2C subunit containing N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor subtypes (GluN1/GluN2A and/or GluN1/Glun2C receptors) are activated during synaptic transmission in hippocampal slices from wild type (WT) mice.
GluN2-B NMDARs mediate pathophysiology in the hippocampus during early pathology in an AD model, and that this is due to aberrant Glu2B NMDAR function during synaptic plasticity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of NMDA receptors (NMDARs) in synaptic plasticity, a cellular mechanism thought to underlie learning and memory.
the role of NMDAR subunits in synaptic function and the development of novel therapeutics for the treatment of Alzheimer's Disease (AD).
the function of NMDA receptors (NMDARs) in the hippocampus during early pathology in an AD mouse model
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GluN2A- and GluN2C-NMDARs, but not GluN2D-NMDARs or GluN2-2B-NMDA receptors, contribute to LTP induction in CA1 pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus.
GluN2A-NMDARs mediate synaptic plasticity during the early phase of Aβ accumulation in the PS2APPS mice.
GluN2b-NMDARs mediate pathophysiology in early stages of AD pathology, and that this is due to a combination of altered GluN subunit expression and function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the GluN2A and GluN2C NMDAR subtypes are not affected by Aβ in the PS2 APP mouse model, but the GluN1/GluN2B NDMAR subtype is affected.
NMDARs are altered in the PS2 APP mouse model of early AD, and that the NMDAR GluN2 subunit plays a critical role in this process.
GluN2A-NMDARs mediate LTP in PS2APP and WT mice, but GluN2NMDARs mediating LTP are altered in PS2APP compared to WT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NMDAR function is altered early in AD, and that NMDARs are a potential therapeutic target in early AD.
GluN2 subtypes of NMDAR play a critical role in synaptic function and synaptic plastic mechanisms in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease (Alzheimer's disease) pathogenesis.

GluN2A-NMDARs mediate LTP in wild type mice, while in the PS2-APP model, GluN2b-NMDARs play the main role in LTP, which is consistent with our previous work showing that GluN1 subunit containing N-MDARs are up-regulated in this model.
